title: Embracing the Rave
summary: Stu Mackenzie and Joey Walker discuss the band’s improvised modular rave set, upcoming orchestral performances and the possibilities opened by playing without a fixed script.
transcript:
Stu Mackenzie and Joey Walker of King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios, the day before the band's first Australian rave set, a free show at Federation Square. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 23 October 2025.

Simon: And of course, as you mentioned at the top, Lauren, 27 albums in so far, not counting all of the, I suppose, unofficials and the bootlegs. And I guess throughout the course of 15 years, have built a really vast catalogue of albums. But even more than that, something of a musical universe, I guess, the Gizzverse that people would know. And sometimes the albums that you produce, I suppose, well, always follow their own path. You've got your own label, p(doom) Records, which enables you to explore microtonal rock, thrash metal, long-form jazz improvisation and so much more.

But of course, the most recent album, Phantom Island, that we were just listening to, came out in June with some beautiful orchestral arrangements, which is just stunning. And we couldn't be more excited to hear that you've got some electronic rave sets that you've been developing, too. This is going to be the first one tomorrow night in Australia at Fed Square, DJ Merve supporting. But yeah, we're so excited. And we want to ask you about where this idea was born, this new chapter of electronic rave music.

Guest: Sick. It's probably been… Thanks for the very epic intro as well. We just make music mostly, which makes sense. But it's been something that has been coming together for a few years, and then also simmering away in the background for probably quite a lot of years before that as well. And I think we probably had this goal to try and figure out how to make live improvised techno with six people, which seems hard and is extremely hard. It actually is hard. So I think we're starting to find the spot within that universe that makes sense for us to [Unclear audio at 00:02:18–00:02:28], I think.

Host: By coincidence, I guess, the week that you're planning your first local rave set, Tame Impala dropped their new rave album as well. It feels like, I don't know, there's something in the air at the moment. Were you channelling a feeling of needing to dance and release energy?

Joey: I mean, yes and no. It has, as you said, been simmering away. Butterfly 3000, there wasn't a single acoustic instrument on that record. It's all just synthesisers. But it wasn't a dance album. And then I guess the [Unclear audio at 00:03:05–00:03:12] remix album was amazing. The artists that came aboard for that, which is crazy.

And then during the pandemic, I got into Eurorack modular synthesising, which is kind of something that has been an endgame for me for a really long time. That's the format. For people out there, it's just the funny-looking synth with heaps of cables on it. It's synthesiser guts, cables on the outside.

So, I guess during a normal Gizzard show, I would have my little Eurorack synth on stage, and I'd contribute in that way. And then we made the record The Silver Cord, which kind of was this, I don't know, Frankenstein genre of electronic music, which ended up being whatever that was. And then I guess Stu kind of inevitably… I was like, 'Man, this modular thing seems like…' [Unclear audio at 00:04:04–00:04:12]

Stu: And I was like, 'Nah, it's boring. Stop talking about it all the time.'

Joey: And then classic Stu just kind of started from nothing, and now could have a modular synthesis YouTube channel dedicated to it.

Host: We heard that it's hard to find you outside of exploring synthesisers at the moment. You're spending most of your days in front of them. I guess you have said that your recent obsession with Eurorack modular synthesis feels like discovering guitar as a teenager all over again. Is that right?

Stu: Yeah, it does. I had this realisation that the feeling is really similar to when I first started playing guitar, and it just felt like the universe was massive and that you could do anything with this instrument. And that's how I remember feeling as a teenager, first learning to play guitar. And I think that I have that same feeling now, and it's good. I kind of try and chase that, actually, making music. And it's cool when you latch onto something like that. I remember when we started doing microtonal music, there was a similar feeling of the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow sort of thing. But yeah, we try to chase that thing.

Host: And what does it look like and sound like in the studio with you when you're messing with these cables? I have an impression of what Eurorack modular synthesis looks like, but in your world, what does it look like? Is it controlled chaos?

Joey: Really funny. It's like a crime scene. It's so hectic. Our sound guy, who lives in Byron Bay, arrived today for the show tomorrow, and he just walked in and he was just like, 'Oh my God.' But yeah, we all are on a table, a big table, and we have our A-frame modular, each of our synths A-frame together. So me and Stu are back to back. It's a giant pyramid. Yeah, it's a pyramid.

And then Ambrose and Cookie are kind of joined, and Lucas is on the end of the table as well. And then Cavs, the drummer, is on the kit. And he was kind of the last to the party, where he was just like, 'Shut up.' But then Stu's just built him a little drum machine Eurorack kit. And Cavs, he's like, 'All right, all right.' Kind of walked into the studio and caught him just trying to get a patch cable, and he turned around and he was so embarrassed. But no, we're all there.

So the thing, I guess, is we have our songs that we're playing that would be from The Silver Cord, or some other songs that we're retrofitting to this setup, and they're in a very simple form. It's maybe a key melody that everyone's receiving, but that is maybe the binding sinew to the song. But outside of that, it's completely improvised in the moment. And the great thing with modular is that it's very generative. We don't want to go into a tech deep dive here, but essentially it's really good at manifesting and creating melody and rhythm and whatever, pulling it out of thin air, really.

So it's kind of like a dance with each other, of how we interact in that moment, and it's hard enough doing that with one person, let alone two, but with six people doing it, it's a lot. It's a dance to let things breathe and all that stuff. So it's been really good. And I feel like we're at a really exciting point with it all. And it also feels infinite, I feel like, in terms of where we can take it. But yeah, we're nervous for tomorrow, but we're excited.

Host: And I guess, in addition to this rave set, you've been touring these three distinct shows simultaneously: the rock, orchestral and these electronic rave sets. You'll be back in December for the orchestra show on December 12, and then there's the next night as well, which is more of a rock show. Can you tell us the difference, I guess, between them from your perspective, maybe in terms of even the preparation and performance aspects behind them?

Guest: The orchestra shows are, I feel like for us as a band, probably furthest from what we're used to. We have to play to charts, and we've got 30-odd people behind us who are playing to a script, which is not the way we tend to operate. So we've worked out a really fun way of doing it, though, because we've done quite a few of the orchestra shows now. But yeah, we have to be more of a cog in the machine. And that's fun. It's actually discipline. It's different. It requires discipline. Whereas the usual show is not discipline-based. It's actually a lack of discipline that usually works the best with the band.

Joey: And one thing I realised as well with the orchestra show versus a traditional Gizzard show is when we were on tour a month or two ago in America, doing primarily the orchestra stuff, but then we'd have a normal rock show in between. Going into the orchestra thing, it was very unfamiliar. We didn't know what to expect. We were all very nervous, dealing with these professional musicians and stuff like that. But once we got over that initial feeling, and realising that is what it is, once we're there, we don't have to really worry about it. The variables aren't as much of a thing.

And then going into a normal Gizzard show, I was like, 'Oh wow, the amount of work,' I guess mental work, at least how I feel going into a Gizzard show, because it's so last minute; every set's different. Tonight Stu will be like, 'We're going to play this song.' I don't even know what that song was called. I haven't heard that song in however long. So there's so much energy put into a normal Gizzard show that I think at the end of the day really pays off for us, and hopefully for the audience, that frenetic, chaotic feel to it. But it was interesting to see that duality between this very regimented orchestral thing and a normal Gizzard show. It was cool. It's refreshing, I think.

Host: And you worked with, I think it was, conductor Sarah Hicks, and there's the composer and music director Chad Kelly as well on the orchestra tour. How did they change how you think about your own music?

Guest: Yeah, I've actually known Chad for quite a few years. Our wives are friends, actually. And so I met Chad just at dinner parties and stuff like that. Chad's a Manchester chap who married an Aussie, but he's a conductor and a composer and such an incredible musician. And we would get together on these dinner party dates and talk about microtonal music and dorky stuff like that. And it was really rad. But we do very much exist on very opposite ends of the musical spectrum. I think we are both interested in deeply dorky stuff, which is where we connected. But I'm a musical idiot, and he's a smart musical person. But we fight, we meet in the middle.

But anyway, we had some opportunities to play some live shows in the States with an orchestra. And the idea was to retrofit the back catalogue and do some shows with some amazing top orchestras in the States. And of course we were just like, 'Well, we have to take that. What a cool opportunity.' So the first person I called was Chad, to get his take on the whole thing. And I think after speaking with him and after brainstorming a little bit, it just became obvious that if we want to do one show, we may as well do a tour. And if we're going to do a tour, we may as well make an album. And so Chad really helped with the whole process, and he wrote the charts for Phantom Island and what became of that. And he's touring with us in Europe as the conductor for the shows.

Guest: And Sarah Hicks did the US stuff, and she's so incredible as well. I have so much respect for conductors now. I just never knew what they were doing with their little magic wands. But now I feel like I do, and it's an incredible job, being able to communicate with all of the different musicians, and especially working with a rock band, that they have to understand what we are all doing. It's like understanding different languages.

Guest: And Sarah is such an amazing conductor. She had this ability to relay this information to every person in a different language, essentially, one by one. It's very cool. Very, very impressive skill.

Host: And you've also been playing in some pretty special places in Europe recently. Back in May you played, I think it was a former prison in Lithuania that's been converted into a music venue. Can we ask about the logistics of that? And also, I guess, what the selection process is like for choosing these locations for your shows?

Guest: I mean, the logistics: kind of like, let's do a tour that's destination-based. And in terms of the intensity of what that tour was like, we did five different places, three nights in each place. So for us, it was pretty low impact, which was really nice, to just be in a place. And they were really amazing places. So actually it was kind of good for the old mental health.

Host: Because you'd be accustomed to travelling rapidly to places.

Guest: It's just the stereotype of waking up in a car park type thing, in the bus behind the venue, and you have no idea where you are. Yeah, it's kind of weird. But yeah, that was really cool. It was just really, really amazing. The venues brought so much energy to the shows. We did the one, Lycabettus Hill, which was the second highest point in Athens, other than the hill that the Acropolis is on. And just up there at sunset, it was just insane how cool it was.

Host: Briefly, we would like to flip to talking about some of the recordings that you've been working on. And of course, Phantom Island was the most recent record, written during the same sessions as Flight b741. You've described the process of making Phantom Island as adding a new colour and energy to the songs. You've talked a bit about your experience with, I suppose, the musical directors and the composers, Sarah Hicks and Chad Kelly. But can you talk a little bit more about the themes and ideas that you're exploring on this record?

Guest: I mean, yeah, musically, it was very cool to work with an orchestra. It does actually feel like you're painting with, let's say, a different set of colours, especially to a rock band. And the stuff that we were doing on that record was pretty bare bones. We were thinking back to basics. There's no guitar pedals, sort of just, we were saying, the music that comes out of your fingertips. It's just trying to be simple and trying to be the organic version of the guitar and that sort of thing. And having so many different colours and sounds to play with in the orchestra is very, very cool. But yeah, Chad Kelly arranged amazing stuff for it.

Guest: I feel like, thematically, it's pretty obvious. But it's kind of just talking about up to where we are now. Just how transient, I guess, our lives have become and stuff. And we all have families, for the most part. So it's a little bit of an examination of that kind of thing. Felt pretty honest and personal for a record for us, I think. And we're probably challenging ourselves and each other to see how earnest you could get away with on a rock track like that.

Host: I guess in terms of challenging each other, or challenging yourselves, perhaps. In the past, you've said that [Unclear audio at 00:16:48–00:16:55], you deliberately make yourself uncomfortable creatively, like using cheap gear. You're forcing yourselves into these unfamiliar genres as well. Is that still the case? Or are there other strategies or techniques you use to maintain creativity and your prolific output?

Guest: Well, I mean, for this record, I definitely didn't tell Chad or any of the orchestral players at the time, but we mixed down to an 8-track cassette tape, which is a very cool machine from the 80s, which is extremely broken. But yeah, thinking about an extremely hi-fi, big orchestra, and we recorded it properly this time. By the way, we mixed down to a tiny cassette. And that actually felt like a huge challenge. And it was kind of the game. The game was to see how you could get the tape to sound as good as possible, actually. So it's just, I don't know why I do this.

Guest: There's also a little bit of trying to subvert doing an orchestral record. It comes with its own kind of… not baggage, but it has a feeling to it. You're like, 'Okay, that's that.' And very often, when a band or bands do that, it can really not be their best work. So I feel like there was a little bit of a subversion into, like, let's garage-ify it. You know what I mean? Which is cool. If it was this ultra hi-fi kind of thing, I just think it might have, I don't know, lost a bit of its soul, or at least a bit of our spirit. I think that it's always trying to inject the Gizzard thing into it.

Guest: It was also genuinely a very, very hard record to finish. And I think it had a bit to do with the combination: we were in blues band formation, really, and fusing that with a small orchestra. I think we had 30-odd people in the studio for the orchestral recording. So it was really hard to make that fit. And I think this slightly sadistic way of mixing a record made it make sense, actually. And it made it live in the same world.

Guest: And I think also, back to your initial question, in terms of creative impetus or whatever: b741 and Phantom Island, same session in terms of the original tracks that were on both those albums. But that was a response to this little scene of albums that we'd had, which were very jammy and nebulous. And the process was a lot of post-production distillation of these huge, expansive jams that we'd do, and then trying to form these, build these songs out of it. So it was like, 'Okay, once we'd gotten through that, we just want to make a song with a couple of chords.' And that's what that is.

And then so now, coming out the other side of that, everyone has absurd modular synthesisers. You know what I mean? So it is that thing. We are chasing — once something's cauterised, we kind of try and do the opposite, or what feels the most exciting.

Simon: I guess there's been, is it 27 albums in the last 14, 15 years or so? You've covered, as I mentioned earlier, so many genres, from thrash metal, synth pop, jazz, electronic rave. Is there a genre you're excited, or perhaps also are you scared, to attempt?

Guest: I think for the most part we probably aren't thinking in terms of genre. I mean, maybe we are occasionally. I think we are genuinely chasing that feeling. We're chasing the dragon of the hard thing, probably, or the thing that would make us, yeah, scared a little bit, or motivated enough to, yeah, just, I don't know.

Joey: It can kind of manifest in a technical side. So, being scared of the learning curve that comes with learning how to use a modular synth. I have a background in dance music or electronic music, and Stu's just got hyper-focused. But a lot of the other guys, it's like, 'I guess we're doing modular synthesis now.' So there's trying to inject some form of learning curve that is cool to try and tackle.

Guest: I think it's trying to put in these restrictions, but barriers within a framework, that once we decide, 'Okay, cool, this album might be metal, or it might be ultra-proggy, or it might be electronic,' we just set these things. There's all channels or lanes in between that. If we try and narrow —

Guest: Yeah, make it make sense.

Guest: And once we realise what that is, that's when we're like, 'Let's make the album.' And then it happens really quickly, because it's almost like working out what we're not doing. Sometimes there can be a lot of time before we start anything, or we just talk about it and figure out what exactly the intent is. It's also just sometimes fun to just burn the house down and start again. And, yeah, I think there's an element of that, too.

Host: Well, it is so thrilling to be a fan of your work, because there is always that sense of exhilaration, excitement and entering into the unknown. I suppose something that we wanted to talk to you about before we let you go is the community that you have really built through your tireless work ethic. I suppose weirdoswarm.org is one of the places where people track the shows they've attended. They organise meet-ups, they run charity events, and participate in an annual gift exchange called Gizzmas. It's a beautiful community that you've built over so many years. We were just wondering how much you get to engage with that at all, and where that fits within your, I suppose, working schedules.

Guest: For me, when you talk about that stuff, it is pretty abstract for the most part. It is actually quite a strange and unreal concept to truly understand. And I feel like the thing I have said before, especially when we were talking about the record b741, which had a lot of flying-on-planes metaphors: a lot of it does feel like being in an aeroplane. If you actually think about the fact that you are in the sky, you actually might have a panic attack. And I think playing to the kind of audiences that we're lucky enough to play to now, I have to abstract myself from it, because it just actually doesn't do any good to think too hard about what the broader ecosystem is.

However, I do really like talking to people, and I'll always try and chat with folks and get a sense of what is going on on the ground.

Guest: And that's when it feels real.

Guest: I think we do, yeah. That is our interaction. We do have a lot of people across the world who might be figures within the Gizz fan community, who we honestly do talk to; they talk to our managers, we talk to them. There's an exchange of relationship.

But for the most part, I think, as to the whole lore, L-O-R-E lore, of the whole thing, I think if we were to actually stop and engage, it would kind of cease to exist. And I think we just let it exist, and it's there because we're not engaging with it. We're just doing our thing. And we just like making music with each other. It's as simple as that. We actually just like being in the same room as each other and making music together. That's the thing.
